questions.q: Added value is…
o: the price minus the cost of bought-in materials
questions.why: It measures what the business adds to its inputs.

questions.q: A social enterprise…
o: has social or environmental aims and reinvests profit to meet them
questions.why: It can make profits but uses them for its social purpose.

questions.q: Which is an internal stakeholder?
questions.why: Internal stakeholders are within the organisation: employees, managers, owners.

questions.q: A business has revenue of $500 000. It spends $320 000 on bought-in materials and services and $100 000 on wages. What is its added value?
questions.why: Added value = revenue − cost of bought-in materials and services = 500 000 − 320 000 = $180 000; wages are paid out of added value, not deducted to find it.

questions.q: A government privatises its state-owned railway company. What is the most likely change in the business's main objective?
o: From earning profit to providing a free service
From serving shareholders to serving only the government
No change, because the same managers remain
From providing a public service to earning a return for private shareholders
questions.why: Once in the private sector the business is owned by shareholders, who usually expect profit, which may conflict with unprofitable public services.

long.q: Explain two differences between a private limited company and a public limited company.
scheme: B1: a public limited company can sell shares to the public on a stock exchange
B1: a private limited company can only sell shares privately, with the agreement of other shareholders
B1: a public company must publish more detailed accounts
B1: so it can raise much more capital but risks takeover

long.q: Explain what is meant by a SMART objective, and write a SMART objective for a car-hire business.
scheme: B1: SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic (or Relevant) and Time-bound
B1: such an objective gives a clear target against which performance can be checked
B1: an example with a number and a deadline, e.g. increase bookings by 10% within 12 months

long.q: A food manufacturer plans a backward vertical merger with a farming business that supplies its vegetables. Analyse two possible benefits to the manufacturer.
scheme: B1: one benefit, e.g. control over the supply and quality of vegetables
B1: analysed, e.g. fewer production delays and more consistent quality, protecting the brand
B1: a second benefit, e.g. the supplier's profit margin is absorbed, so costs fall / rivals' access to supplies can be restricted
B1: analysed, e.g. lower costs raise profit margins or allow lower prices

long.q: Evaluate whether a clothing retailer should adopt a policy of corporate social responsibility (CSR). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: CSR defined: a business considering the interests of all stakeholders and society, not just shareholders
B1: applied, e.g. paying fair wages to factory workers abroad / using sustainable cotton / reducing packaging
B1: benefit analysed: better reputation and brand image attracts ethically minded customers, so sales rise
B1: benefit analysed: easier to recruit and keep staff / less risk of boycotts and bad publicity
B1: cost analysed: higher costs reduce profit or force higher prices
B1: cost analysed: price-sensitive customers may switch to cheaper rivals that do not adopt CSR
B1: evaluation: depends on, e.g. its target market, how competitive the market is, whether the policy is genuine
B1: a supported judgement on whether it should adopt CSR

long.q: Explain two reasons why small businesses are important to an economy.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. they create many jobs
B1: explained, e.g. often in local areas or for people larger firms do not employ
B1: a second reason, e.g. they bring competition and innovation / supply larger firms / may grow into large firms
B1: explained, e.g. competition keeps prices down and gives consumers choice

questions.q: Herzberg's hygiene factors…
o: cause dissatisfaction if absent but don't motivate
questions.why: Motivators include recognition, responsibility and achievement.

questions.q: Labour turnover is…
o: the percentage of staff leaving in a period
questions.why: (Number leaving ÷ average number employed) × 100.

questions.q: Which motivation theory separates hygiene factors from motivators?
questions.why: Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction but don't motivate.

questions.q: A business had an average of 250 employees during the year and 30 of them left. What is its labour turnover?
questions.why: Labour turnover = staff leaving ÷ average number employed × 100 = 30 ÷ 250 × 100 = 12%.

questions.q: A manager breaks jobs into simple tasks, pays workers per item produced and supervises them closely to raise output. Whose ideas does this approach reflect?
questions.why: Taylor's scientific management assumed workers are motivated mainly by money and favoured simple tasks, piece rates and close control.

long.q: Explain two non-financial methods a manager could use to motivate employees.
scheme: B1: one method, e.g. job enrichment / job rotation / empowerment / team working
B1: explained, e.g. more responsible, varied work meets higher-level needs (Maslow, Herzberg's motivators)
B1: a second method, e.g. recognition / training / delegation
B1: explained, e.g. employees feel valued, so effort and retention rise

long.q: A business had an average of 400 employees during the year and 36 of them left. Calculate its labour turnover and explain two possible consequences of high labour turnover.
scheme: B1: one consequence, e.g. higher recruitment and training costs
B1: a second consequence, e.g. loss of skills and experience / lower productivity and quality while new staff learn / lower morale

long.q: Explain the difference between Taylor's and Mayo's views of how to motivate workers.
scheme: B1: Taylor: workers are motivated mainly by money
B1: so jobs are broken into simple tasks, closely supervised and paid by piece rate
B1: Mayo: workers are motivated by social needs, e.g. team working and the attention of managers (Hawthorne effect)
B1: so managers should communicate with workers, consult them and build teams

long.q: Analyse two benefits to a business of carrying out regular employee appraisal.
scheme: B1: one benefit, e.g. identifies training needs
B1: analysed, e.g. training then targets the skills employees lack, so productivity rises
B1: a second benefit, e.g. sets targets and gives feedback / identifies staff for promotion / motivates by recognising good work
B1: analysed, e.g. employees feel valued, so motivation rises and labour turnover falls

long.q: Evaluate whether a democratic leadership style is always the most suitable style for the manager of a hospital emergency department. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: democratic leadership defined: the manager involves employees in decisions and discusses ideas with them
B1: autocratic (or laissez-faire) defined as an alternative
B1: benefit of democratic style analysed: skilled staff such as doctors and nurses contribute expertise, giving better decisions
B1: benefit analysed: staff feel valued, so motivation and retention improve
B1: drawback analysed: consultation takes time, which may not be possible in an emergency
B1: in a crisis an autocratic style gives quick, clear instructions
B1: evaluation: the best style depends on the situation, the urgency of decisions and the skills of the staff
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. democratic for planning and routine matters, autocratic during emergencies

questions.q: In the product life cycle, sales grow fastest during…
questions.why: Sales rise rapidly as the product gains acceptance.

questions.q: Market segmentation means…
o: dividing a market into groups of customers with similar needs
questions.why: Segments can be based on age, income, location or lifestyle.

questions.q: What does a price elasticity of demand of −0.4 mean?
o: Demand is price inelastic, so raising price raises revenue
questions.why: Apply it: say what it means for this business's revenue.

questions.q: A firm raises its price from $20 to $22 and quantity demanded falls from 1 000 to 850 units. What is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.why: PED = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price = −15% ÷ +10% = −1.5, so demand is price elastic.

questions.q: A holiday company designs separate packages for thrill-seekers and for customers who value luxury and relaxation, whatever their age or income. Which type of segmentation is this?
questions.why: Psychographic segmentation groups customers by lifestyle, attitudes and personality rather than by age, income or location.

long.q: Explain two elements of the marketing mix a business could use to launch a new smartphone.
scheme: B1: one element identified, e.g. price (penetration or skimming)
B1: explained in context, e.g. skimming earns high profit from early adopters
B1: a second element, e.g. promotion (social media, influencers) or place (online and retail)
B1: explained in context, e.g. reaching young buyers where they shop

long.q: Total market sales rose from $40 million to $46 million in a year, while a firm's sales rose from $6 million to $6.6 million. Calculate the market growth rate and the firm's market share in each year, and comment on the firm's performance.
scheme: A1: market share year 1 = 6 ÷ 40 × 100 = 15%
A1: market share year 2 = 6.6 ÷ 46 × 100 = 14.3%
B1: comment: the firm's sales grew by 10%, but more slowly than the market, so it lost market share to rivals

long.q: Average incomes rise by 4% and the demand for a restaurant's meals rises by 10%. Calculate the income elasticity of demand and explain what it means for the restaurant.
scheme: B1: the meals are a normal, income-elastic (luxury) good: sales rise strongly when incomes rise but would fall sharply in a recession

long.q: Explain two sampling methods a market researcher could use.
scheme: B1: one method, e.g. random sampling
B1: explained: every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen, which reduces bias
B1: a second method, e.g. quota / stratified / cluster / snowball sampling
B1: explained, e.g. quota: a set number from each group (age, gender) is chosen to match the target market

long.q: Analyse how a business with several products could use the Boston matrix to manage its product portfolio.
scheme: B1: the matrix classifies products by market share and market growth
B1: into stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs
B1: cash cows (high share, low growth) earn cash that can fund other products
B1: question marks need investment and promotion to become stars, or should be dropped
B1: dogs (low share, low growth) may be withdrawn to free resources
B1: so the business can keep a balanced portfolio, with products at different stages, spreading risk and cash flow

questions.q: Capacity utilisation is…
questions.why: High utilisation spreads fixed costs; very high leaves no slack.

questions.q: Just-in-time inventory management aims to…
o: receive inputs only as they are needed
questions.why: It cuts storage costs but depends on reliable suppliers.

questions.q: Why does more output not guarantee more profit?
o: Goods may not be sold, and extra output adds costs
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common assumption was that more output guarantees more sales and profits.

questions.q: Which best describes kaizen?
o: Holding large buffer inventories in case demand rises
Continuous small improvements, often suggested by the workers themselves
Producing goods only when an order is received
questions.why: Kaizen is a lean production approach in which many small, ongoing changes, usually from employees, improve quality and efficiency.

questions.q: A hotel has 80 rooms and on average 60 are occupied each night. To reach 90% capacity utilisation without adding rooms, how many rooms must be occupied on average?
questions.why: 90% of the maximum capacity of 80 rooms = 0.9 × 80 = 72 rooms.

long.q: A factory can make 5000 units a month and makes 3500. Calculate its capacity utilisation and explain one problem of operating at this level.
scheme: B1: fixed costs are spread over fewer units, so the average cost per unit is higher (or idle resources, lower morale)

long.q: A business uses 200 units of a component a day. The supplier's lead time is 4 days, the buffer inventory is 300 units and the maximum inventory level is 2000 units. Calculate the re-order level and the re-order quantity.
scheme: M1: usage during the lead time = 200 × 4 = 800 units
A1: re-order level = 300 + 800 = 1100 units
M1: re-order quantity = maximum inventory − buffer inventory

long.q: A factory produced 24 000 units with 60 workers last year. This year it produced 27 000 units with 54 workers. Calculate the percentage change in labour productivity.
scheme: M1: productivity last year = 24 000 ÷ 60 = 400 units per worker
M1: this year = 27 000 ÷ 54 = 500 units per worker

long.q: Evaluate whether a smartphone manufacturer should outsource the production of its components. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: outsourcing defined: using another business to carry out an activity instead of doing it in-house
B1: applied to components such as screens, chips or batteries
B1: benefit analysed: specialist suppliers have economies of scale and expertise, so costs may be lower
B1: benefit analysed: frees capital and management time for design and marketing / more flexible capacity
B1: drawback analysed: less control over quality, which could damage the brand
B1: drawback analysed: risk of late deliveries / supplier failure / loss of confidential designs
B1: evaluation: depends on, e.g. supplier reliability, how central the component is to the product's competitive advantage
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. outsource standard components but keep key technology in-house

long.q: Explain two diseconomies of scale a rapidly growing business might suffer.
scheme: B1: one diseconomy, e.g. poor communication
B1: explained: longer chains of command mean messages are slow or distorted, so mistakes rise and average costs increase
B1: a second diseconomy, e.g. poor coordination / control / low morale and motivation of workers who feel unimportant
B1: explained with how it raises average costs

questions.q: Working capital is…
questions.why: It funds day-to-day operations.

questions.q: Profit and cash differ because…
o: sales on credit count as revenue before cash is received
questions.why: Timing differences mean a profitable business can run out of cash.

questions.q: Which is a full definition of fixed costs?
o: Costs that do not change with the level of output in the short run
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many gave only a partial definition such as 'costs that do not change'.

questions.q: What is a cash-flow forecast used for?
o: Predicting future cash inflows and outflows to spot shortfalls
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates continue to believe cash-flow forecasts calculate profit.

questions.q: Net cash flow is calculated as:
questions.why: Examiners (2023): errors often came from subtracting inflows from outflows rather than the other way round.

questions.q: ARR uses which figure for investment?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many did not calculate the average investment and so got the ARR wrong.

long.q: A business has fixed costs of $24 000 a month. It sells its product for $20 and the variable cost is $12 a unit. Calculate the break-even output and the margin of safety when it sells 4000 units.
scheme: M1: contribution per unit = $20 − $12 = $8
A1: break-even = 24 000 ÷ 8 = 3000 units
M1: margin of safety = 4000 − 3000
A1: = 1000 units

long.q: A business has current assets of $45 000, of which $15 000 is inventory, and current liabilities of $30 000. Calculate its current ratio and acid test ratio.
scheme: M1: current ratio = 45 000 ÷ 30 000

long.q: A business has an opening cash balance of $5000. Its forecast cash inflows for the next three months are $12 000, $14 000 and $9000, and its forecast cash outflows are $15 500, $13 000 and $11 000. Calculate the closing balance for each month and explain one limitation of a cash-flow forecast.
scheme: B1: limitation, e.g. figures are estimates: sales may be lower, or customers pay late, or costs rise unexpectedly

long.q: A business budgeted for revenue of $80 000 and costs of $60 000 in a month. Actual revenue was $76 000 and actual costs $57 500. Calculate the revenue, cost and profit variances, stating whether each is favourable or adverse.
scheme: B1: revenue variance = $4000 adverse
B1: cost variance = $2500 favourable
M1: budgeted profit = $20 000; actual profit = $18 500
A1: profit variance = $1500 adverse
long.ans: Revenue $4000 A; costs $2500 F; profit $1500 A

long.q: Evaluate whether a growing private limited company should finance a new factory with a long-term bank loan or by selling new shares. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a bank loan is debt finance: repaid with interest over an agreed period
B1: new shares are equity finance: sold to new or existing shareholders, with no repayment
B1: loan analysed: the owners keep control, but interest must be paid even if profits fall, and gearing rises
B1: loan analysed: security may be needed; rising interest rates increase costs
B1: shares analysed: no interest, but dividends are expected and ownership is diluted
B1: shares analysed: a private company can only sell shares privately, so may struggle to raise enough
B1: evaluation: depends on, e.g. current gearing, interest rates, the owners' wish to keep control, the factory's expected returns
B1: a supported judgement on the better source

questions.q: A SWOT analysis looks at…
questions.why: Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats external.

questions.q: Ansoff's matrix: selling new products in new markets is…
questions.why: It is the riskiest strategy.

questions.q: Investment appraisal: net present value accounts for…
questions.why: Future cash flows are discounted to present values.

questions.q: An option costs $50 000 and has a 0.6 probability of earning $100 000 and a 0.4 probability of earning $20 000. Using a decision tree, what is the net expected value?
questions.why: Expected value = 0.6 × 100 000 + 0.4 × 20 000 = $68 000; subtracting the $50 000 cost gives $18 000.

questions.q: A firm aims to have the lowest costs in its industry so that it can compete on price across the whole market. Which of Porter's generic strategies is this?
questions.why: Cost leadership targets the broad market with the lowest unit costs; focus targets a niche, and diversification is an Ansoff growth option, not a Porter strategy.

long.q: Evaluate whether a business should use Porter's generic strategies to compete in a new overseas market.
scheme: B1: cost leadership, differentiation or focus explained
B1: applied to the business's strengths and the market
B1: limits: hybrid strategies, local conditions
B1: a supported judgement

long.q: A project costs $50 000 and returns $15 000 a year for five years. Calculate the payback period and the average rate of return (ARR).
scheme: A1: = 3.33 years (3 years 4 months)
M1: average annual profit = (75 000 − 50 000) ÷ 5 = 5000

long.q: A project costs $120 000 and is expected to generate net cash inflows of $40 000 in each of the next four years. The discount factors at 10% are 0.909, 0.826, 0.751 and 0.683. Calculate the net present value and explain what it shows.
scheme: B1: positive, so the project earns more than the 10% cost of capital and is worth considering, though the cash flows are only forecasts

long.q: A business must choose between two options. Option A costs $200 000 and has a 0.7 probability of earning $500 000 and a 0.3 probability of earning $100 000. Option B costs $80 000 and has a 0.5 probability of earning $250 000 and a 0.5 probability of earning $150 000. Use expected values to recommend an option, and state one limitation of this method.
scheme: A1: net expected value of A = 380 000 − 200 000 = $180 000
A1: net expected value of B = 200 000 − 80 000 = $120 000, so choose A
B1: limitation, e.g. the probabilities and earnings are estimates / A is riskier, with a possible loss of $100 000 / ignores qualitative factors

long.q: A long-established manufacturer plans to introduce automated production, but many employees oppose the change. Evaluate how the business could manage this resistance to change. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: reasons for resistance identified, e.g. fear of job losses, loss of status, uncertainty, need to learn new skills
B1: method analysed: communicate early and explain why the change is needed (e.g. to stay competitive)
B1: method analysed: involve employees and their representatives in planning the change, so they gain ownership
B1: method analysed: training and support, so employees can use the new technology
B1: method analysed: introduce the change gradually / offer retraining or redeployment rather than redundancy
B1: a limitation, e.g. consultation takes time and costs money; some job losses may be unavoidable
B1: evaluation: success depends on, e.g. the corporate culture, trust in management, leadership style, the scale of the change
B1: a supported judgement on the most effective approach
